newsitem.title: MEXICO: With competition at gate, Telmex Q3 mixed.
newsitem.headline: With competition at gate, Telmex Q3 mixed.

text.p: Mexican telephone giant Telefonos de Mexico SA's third quarter results gave investors a mixed picture of the company's ability to weather a storm of upcoming competition, analysts said on Friday.

Revenues jumped a healthy 11.4 percent year-on-year, but anemic line growth of just 0.9 percent on a yearly basis caused worry that a weak local economy will hurt Telmex's local business just as it gears up to face a horde of new competitors in the lucrative long-distance business January 1.
Telmex shares were off 1.31 percent to 12.30 pesos in late trade on Friday. In New York, its heavily traded ADRs were off 1/2 to 31.
"This is definitely a case of, is the glass half empty or half full?" said Paul Aran, a telecommunications analyst at HSBC James Capel in New York.

Telmex year-on-year results are puzzling and analysts are divided on the reasons for it. Telmex reported a third quarter net profit of 3.560 billion pesos, down 19.8 percent compared to the year-ago period, while operating profits also fell 9.7 percent during the quarter compared to the year-ago quarter.
Some analysts say the slide in earnings was due largely to accounting changes, while the third quarter of 1995 also included charges related to settlement negotiations with future rivals.
However, others believe Telmex allowed its costs to rise too much, in part due to higher advertising as Telmex gears up for competition.
Adjusting for all non-cash gains and losses, Telmex's real cash earnings were only down about 5 percent during the quarter, Bear Stearns analyst Rizwan Ali noted.
Telmex's existing network fell by 17,789 lines during the quarter from the second quarter due to a greater number of disconnections than new customers.
"(The fall in lines) demonstrates the sorry plight of Telmex's core business," wrote Ali in a report on Friday.
Telmex's CFO Adolfo Cerezo told analysts on Friday they should not expect significant line growth anytime soon.

"We shouldn't expect to see anything in terms of growth for the rest of the year ... I hope 1997 will show a change, not in the first quarter, but in the second quarter," Cerezo said during a conference call with analysts.

On a quarterly basis, the results were more encouraging. Operating income rose 19 percent compared to the second quarter while the company's operating margin rose from 35.9 percent at the end of June to 38.3 percent currently.
"The real positive here is when you look at minutes growth: it's very good. Local service revenues were very good without help from the economy," Aran said.
Local revenues rose 6.3 percent compared to the year-ago quarter thanks to an increase in local rates of about 13.5 percent in real terms this year.

Domestic and international long-distance revenues jumped about 20 percent versus last year's third quarter, mostly due to a slightly improving economy and a new discount program started by Telmex in August.
"We believe that Telmex's results are impressive, given the weak operating environment," wrote Leslie Marcus of Santander Investment in a report released on Friday.
Analysts also had different views on Telmex's costs. Some praised management's effort to control costs in the face of weak economy, but others said costs rose too much during the quarter.

Bear Stearns' Ali said cash operating expenses rose 23 percent in real terms, adjusting for accounting changes that Telmex said accounted for the quarter's huge 36.5 percent rise in cash costs versus last year's third quarter.
